The widening of the 90% confidence intervals from the one-day to the one-month horizon reflects the inherent increase in uncertainty as one forecasts further into the future. For the one-day outlook, the interval was narrow, indicating high confidence in outcomes close to the point estimate, influenced mainly by immediate, random fluctuations inherent to any system. As the horizon extended to one week and then one month, the intervals significantly broadened, accounting for a greater accumulation of potential variability. This expansion primarily stems from the compounding effect of minor, unpredictable daily changes, as well as an increased susceptibility to larger, systemic uncertainties that become more likely to manifest over longer periods. These uncertainties could include general market volatility, shifts in underlying conditions, or the natural stochasticity of the system being observed.

While the confidence intervals encompass a wide range of plausible outcomes, certain specific risks or "black swan" events could push actual results beyond these stated bounds. These might include sudden, unforeseen policy changes by regulatory bodies, major economic disruptions such as unexpected recessions or rapid inflation, or significant geopolitical shifts that fundamentally alter global or local conditions. Breakthrough technological developments, widespread natural disasters, or the emergence of entirely new market dynamics could also introduce unprecedented changes. Such high-impact, low-probability events are inherently difficult to quantify within standard probabilistic models, representing extreme deviations that could fundamentally alter the trajectory of the forecasted variable in ways not captured by typical historical patterns or current assumptions.
